引入 EMA 機制：打破歷史包袱與局部最佳解

Without changing a single character of the objective function, they simply rewrote how cluster centers are updated , reducing the training rounds required. to reach the same clustering quality to about one-tenth of the original. In large-scale vector search, clustering is often a prerequisite step for building an index . How often an index can be rebuilt depends directly on how long the clustering takes to run. Taking it a step further, large model inference compresses attention caches and quantizes attention, which also uses methods like K-means, so it’s actually not as far from the frontier as we. imagine. What K-means actually does is simple: it splits a pile of data into K clusters, minimizing the sum of squared distances from each sample to its assigned center. This goal hasn't changed for decades; all the evolution has happened in how to solve it. The most classic method is Lloyd's algorithm , which works in two steps: first assign all samples to the nearest center, then calculate a new center using the mean of each cluster's samples. These two steps repeat until the centers basically stop moving. This process has a binding condition: every time an update is completed, the entire dataset must be scanned once. Therefore, the larger the. data, the more expensive each scan becomes. One round here refers to an epoch, which means going through the entire dataset once. So, rounds and computational load are basically linearly related; cutting nine-tenths of the rounds saves nine-tenths of the data scanning. Open-source Faiss defaults to running 25 rounds, a number that has slowly become an industry benchmark. Many use the error rate of Lloyd's algorithm after 25 rounds as a reference line. But at a scale of 10 billion items , 25 rounds mean extremely expensive repetitive calculations. Taking real-world scenarios, running 1 billion vectors for 25 rounds takes over 6,000.

GPU hours. What about mini-batch updates ? Actually, this approach isn't exactly new. The sequential update proposed by MacQueen in 1967 followed this logic. In 2010, Sculley's MiniBatchKMeans pushed it to web scale, updating centers after processing a portion of samples without waiting for the full pass. It is fast, and the logic sounds much more coherent . Later, others modified it, with solutions emerging for streaming data, concept drift, and noisy mixtures. However, one issue remained unresolved: how to set the parameters. When users. get new data, they still have to guess for themselves. The key problem with batch versus non-batch lies in how statistics are accumulated. Classic mini-batch keeps adding historical statistics, so when early center positions are inaccurate, those allocation records affect results for a long time. Such methods usually converge faster, but the error is higher than in fully trained K-Means. You still have to test batch sizes and learning rates yourself, and repeating this for new data makes speed, quality, and ease of use hard to balance. This optimized K-Means takes a different approach: it. stops accumulating and uses Exponential Moving Averages (EMA) to maintain centers, which is not complex. First, keep two values for each center: the number of samples assigned to it, and the sum of these vectors. The center itself is not stored directly, but calculated as the ratio of these two values. Every time a mini-batch arrives , these two values undergo a moving average based on a decay rate. New assignments can pull the center toward them in a timely manner. Older statistical records gradually lose their weight. One interpretation is that it treats K-Means updates as a hard-assignment EM, but with decaying. statistics. This perspective is not new , but no one had systematically treated the decay rate as a tunable, optimizable variable before. Of course, these rules are not unfamiliar, as this is how codebook updates in VQ-VAE work. Later, neural audio codecs even patched it to pull "dead" centers back to life. The difference is that those cases face a constantly shifting distribution, where the EMA decay rate is basically treated as a constant, and no one adjusts it. But here, we face fixed data with the goal of minimizing error, so the formula.

must be redesigned. The team also compared it against Stochastic Gradient Descent. When training with large batches and large update steps, gradient descent can become unstable. The authors suggest that EMA updates keep centers within the convex hull of assigned samples, effectively limiting jitter caused by large steps. While this explanation isn't a rigorous proof—more of a geometric intuition—the direction is correct. What's more worth noting is how it changes the probability of getting stuck in local optima. L-Lloyd's algorithm reduces training error every round, which sounds good, but it also. means that once it settles, it stays there comfortably and cannot get out on its own. The stochastic fluctuations from mini-batches actually give EMA a chance to readjust, nudging even those centers that have already stabilized. The team conducted an experiment that illustrates this well: data consisting of two clusters of vastly different sizes is to be divided into eight groups . Lloyd's sometimes assigns two centers to the smaller cluster, leaving the larger one short. EMA, starting from the same initial state, has the opportunity to correct itself. In 200 random initializations, Lloyd's got stuck in. these suboptimal groupings 26%of the time, while EMA did so only 3.5%. With five clusters arranged in a line, these rates became 46%and 0%. Note that these experiments used random initialization; they didn't even use K-means ++. Another easily overlooked detail is that in Lloyd's, some centers gradually stop receiving samples during training, effectively wasting that portion of clustering capacity. In contrast, EMA checks every five batches. If a center's sample count falls below a certain ratio of the average, it splits half from a. larger, active cluster to reassign it, rather than just simply picking a random sample. However, this splitting logic follows existing practices from Faiss and isn't a new invention. In ablation experiments, taking the YFCC 1-million sample dataset as an example, disabling the revival mechanism resulted in 26.3% of centers having fewer than 10 samples . Once enabled, this proportion dropped to 0.3%. Also in ablation, replacing revival with simply picking a random sample from the current batch—a cheaper approach—showed significantly worse.

results. The impacts of other modifications, including removing them individually, were mostly on the order of a few tenths of a percentage point. Using K-means ++ initialization can indeed improve things slightly, but it's too expensive; when the epoch budget is tight, you're better off just training for a few more rounds. The remaining adjustments are basically centered around stability and convergence. Initialization involves randomly selecting centers from the data, but assigns a minimal weight to the initial statistics. After the first update, almost no trace remains. The learning rate uses a decay schedule, gradually decreasing from peak to floor, so training doesn't oscillate in the later. stages. Once the final round finishes, you can calculate the centers again using the mean of the samples assigned in that round; the cost is nearly zero, and training error is guaranteed to drop . If these centers are meant for processing new data rather than serving the training set itself, you can attach a slower moving average specifically to improve test error. Moreover, these two finishing methods do not conflict. One training run can yield two sets of centers; which one to use depends on whether you want optimality on the training set or for new samples. If you set the batch size to the full dataset and the step size to one, the moving average degrades into Lloyd's full-batch recalculation. It sounds like taking parameters to the limit brings you back to the start, but in reality, this classic configuration lands right in a poor-performing corner of the error heatmap. The authors ran 75,000 optimization experiments to. distill the relationships between sample size, training rounds, and optimal parameters into two empirical rules. One is used to determine the step size, and the other for the batch size. The definition of batch size is nuanced; they use the "knee point," which is the largest batch size where validation error remains within 0.2 of the curve's minimum, rounded to a power of two. If the scale increases further, this batch size rule needs to be divided by eight, as small batches no longer affect throughput at that point. Interestingly , these two rules were fitted on Deep1B data, yet they transfer well to Sift,.

SpaceV, and text vectors. On held-out data, choosing the default "relatively optimal" parameters via these formulas results in a median error increase of only about 0.19%. The real difficulty lies in the fact that the local intrinsic dimension of the data is usually unknown beforehand, so this rule is more of a good starting point rather than a universal formula ready for immediate use. For the average user, the significance of this is comparable to a performance boost. In the past, when. switching datasets, you either relied on experience to guess, or performed a round of hyperparameter search; now, you just need to provide three numbers— dataset size and number of training rounds—and the parameters appear automatically. It even offers two types of workflows: one focused on throughput and the other on quality, which you can choose based on your scenario. Regarding experiments, the team covered scales from 1 million to 10 billion, using both image and text data on H100s and 64- core Intel Xeons; none of the experiments were tuned for specific datasets. Control groups included FAISS , FlashKMeans, mini-batch versions from. scikit-learn, and other later improvements, while the CPU side also added distance-pruning implementations like SuperKMeans. The evaluation metric is Mean Squared Error (MSE), which is the average squared distance from samples to their nearest centers. Using the test error of FlashKMeans after 25 rounds as the target, Instans reached it in just 1.4 to 2.6 rounds in main comparisons, translating to a real-time speedup of 9.5 to 45.5 times, with the highest peak in the 11 billion DINO vector experiment. On CPUs, the speedup is 9 to 15 times. However, we must clarify the criteria for this multiplier. : it compares who hits the target error of the other’s 25th round first, rather than who is faster when running the same number of rounds. Since the computational load per round is roughly the same, the algorithmic savings are mainly reflected in scanning the data fewer times. Moreover, it’s not just faster; after convergence, its errors in both training and testing are lower than standard methods, including those using KMeans ++ initialization; all eight Instans configurations outperformed FlashKMeans after 25 rounds. If the opponent also uses KMeans ++ initialization, the gap narrows, but after five rounds, Instans is still.

lower; another detail is that if you plot the final errors of 40 random seeds as a histogram, the Instans distribution is overall more shifted to the left. So it wins not by luck in a single instance , but because its overall distribution is more robust. So, why hasn’t it helped much? The author’s explanation is quite practical: this initialization method is serial with no parallel implementation, making it difficult to achieve production-level efficiency. Even discounting its computational cost, the error cannot be recovered on this dataset. This is why the default configuration of InMi initialization requires minimal effort. Beyond real. vectors, the authors used seven synthetic datasets for comparison, including uniform cubes, isotropic Gaussians, stretched Gaussians, and Gaussian mixtures, all yielding conclusions consistent with real data. Fewer rounds translating into actual time savings also depends on engineering implementation; the GPU kernel processes data in blocks, keeping only the nearest candidates rather than writing out the full distance matrix. The assignment step uses low-precision formats like BF16, FP8, or int, and is merged with. the nearest center selection. Fewer rounds is an algorithmic matter, while fewer memory reads is a system matter; the combination leads to the final performance figures. For the 10- billion-scale implementation, the team took 60 million images from YFCC100M and used DINOv3 to extract features as image patches. Each image has 196 vectors of 1024 dimensions, totaling 11.7 billion, with 10 billion remaining after deduplication. The volume after quantization is about 10TB, publicly available via the C 4.0 protocol for. batch downloads, with 1.67 million clusters on this data. Faiss takes 6,784 GPU hours over 25 rounds, using 64 machines. InMi takes only 779 GPU hours over 2.5 rounds, using 32 machines, with even lower error. At this scale, just storing the counts and vector sums for each cluster in float32 takes 64GB of VRAM. So, in the actual implementation, these accumulators must be distributed across VRAM; if the number of clusters reaches a million, distance calculation becomes the bottleneck. At this point,.

one can build an inverted file for the centers, so IV uses a few candidate clusters for each vector instead of comparing against all. By using this approximation, InMi achieves target error in 3 rounds, reducing computation to 23.2 GPU hours. An 8-GPU H100 machine only needs to run for about three hours . Finally, regarding retrieval, clustering is usually just an intermediate step; the quality of centers dictates index performance, so the team tested the new centers against 11 datasets at 1%recall. This dataset. includes classic image descriptors like SIFT, text vectors like SpaceV, and other public index benchmarks; given the same training time, its recall is usually higher. To reach the same recall levels achieved by fully trained traditional methods, it takes significantly less time. Across many datasets, its final recall rate is comparable or better, with its advantages most evident on datasets like SverA and LandmarkDNO. The dataset itself has also been released; as an approximate nearest neighbor benchmark with full ground truth, researchers can use it directly for comparison. The implementation code is now in the Faiss. repository under the module name " ivf_nm," which includes experimental configurations, but since it isn't in a formal release, you'll need to compile it from source. In the author list, you can see core Faiss contributors like Jeff Johnson and Matthijs Douze, which likely explains why the engineering implementation of this work is so meticulous. Overall, what I care about most isn't actually the 45x figure, but rather where it appears. For an algorithm considered long-solved, everyone has spent decades optimizing engineering implementations, such as distance calculations, kernel counts, or parallel strategies; few have looked. back to touch the update rules themselves. Yet, what was changed this time is precisely that part. Exponential moving averages, learning rate decay, and fused kernels are all staples of deep learning, and now they've been applied to a classic optimization problem. The results are, in fact, even more pronounced than in their native scenarios. For teams using Faiss to handle large-scale vectors, the most direct change is the cost of index reconstruction. Previously, the clustering step was very expensive, so updates were infrequent; now that it's an order of magnitude cheaper, update frequencies can be recalculated.

Thanks for watching, we will.

Meta 的 FAIR 团队给用了近 70 年的 K-Means 换了一套中心更新规则，不改目标函数，只把"累加历史统计量"改成指数移动平均，再配上余弦退火、死簇复活和自动调参的缩放定律。结果是 1.4 到 2.6 轮就能达到传统 Lloyd 算法 25 轮的误差，GPU 实际加速 9.5 到 45.5 倍，收敛误差还更低。视频里会讲清这套配方每一步在解决什么问题、为什么两轮反而更准，以及它在百亿向量、1677 万个簇上的真实成绩，最后聊聊聚类变便宜之后，向量索引的更新节奏会被怎么改写。

  • 透過印度員工 Ravi 的遭遇，具體呈現 AI 提升效率如何同時帶來職場淘汰與利益分配不均。
  • 整理 AI 成本下降、資料中心投資激增與模型收入成長之間的矛盾，說明技術成功不必然代表投資人獲利。
  • 從美中競爭與「主權 AI」的角度，解析人工智慧如何從商業產品延伸為國家能力的一部分。
  • 提出「誰掌握通路與金融，誰更可能取得穩定利潤」的核心觀點，提供理解 AI 產業格局的新視角。

摘要

智慧愈便宜，建置成本卻愈高

大飛以兩組看似矛盾的數字開場：同等能力的機器智慧，過去一年單位價格約下降13 倍；另一方面，美國大型雲端業者的資本支出卻快速攀升，去年超過 4,000 億美元，今年接近 8,000 億美元，明年可能突破 1 兆美元。引用 Will Manidis 與 Joe Roberts 的文章《The High Ground》，他指出，智慧本身可能逐漸成為低利潤甚至虧本引流的商品，較穩定的獲利則可能落在掌握通路與金融渠道的人手中：未來要嘛擁有渠道，要嘛付費給渠道的所有者。

Ravi 的故事：效率提升，不等於人人受益

大飛以班加羅爾的 Ravi 為例。他在為美國客戶處理後勤會計的跨境公司工作，十四年來生活穩定，直到公司開始以自動化流程接手更多工作。Ravi 的團隊人數縮減、停止招募，他也從管理同事轉為檢查 AI 代理產出的報告。起初他仔細核對，後來因系統少有錯誤而逐漸只做核准；然而，他反覆核准、退回與修正的紀錄，正好成為系統學習如何取代他的資料。最後，他失去工作，公司支付六個月資遣費，母公司的股價卻在紐約開盤後上漲。這個故事凸顯：企業效率的提升，與成果如何分配，是兩回事。

技術革命的財富，往往流向別處

大飛指出，歷史上，技術發明者不一定是最終的財富受益者。古騰堡發明活字印刷，最後卻破產；鐵路改變美國經濟，最大財富並未落在火車製造商手中，而是流向掌握路權、金融與組織力量的人；電晶體的產業價值，也逐漸集中於半導體製造、設計與電子供應鏈，而非發明它的實驗室。Manidis 與 Roberts 將模型的建置、訓練、評估及推論服務銷售等環節稱為「Genesis」，並承認部署與產業整合或許能長期獲利；他們真正質疑的是，這些利潤能否以足夠快的速度擴散到更廣泛的經濟體系。

成本曲線、資本支出與過度投資風險

依照 Ark Invest 追蹤的指標，達到同等模型表現的最低成本，自 2023 年以來平均每季下降約47%，速度超過光纖、行動網路、電話、電報與鐵路等過往技術；但前沿模型的訓練成本每年約增加 3.5 倍，所需算力年增約 5 倍，晶片可供應的總算力卻只增長約 3.4 倍。於是形成弔詭局面：訓練愈來愈昂貴，推論卻愈來愈便宜，資金仍持續湧入。麥肯錫預估 2030 年資料中心投資將達 7 兆美元，資本支出年增約 70%，遠高於營運現金流約 23% 的增幅，差額須由債務、私人信貸及結構化融資填補。

模型公司的營收確實成長，OpenAI 預計 2026 年底年化營收可達 700 億美元，輝達單季營收也曾大幅增加；但目前營收主要來自早期採用者，AI 在企業流程中的普及仍剛起步，而且使用程度高度不均。OpenAI 企業客戶中，推論用量最高的前 10% 公司，單一活躍用戶用量是中間 10% 的 8.3 倍，高於年初的 2.6 倍。同時，開源模型與最強閉源模型的差距已縮小到約四個月。每家公司繼續投資看似理性，但全體同時擴張，仍可能造成產能過剩與永久性資本損失。

AI 股價、信用擴張與美元購買力

大飛進一步指出，美國經濟成長、家庭財富與信用擴張，正愈來愈繫於同一條線：AI 股票價格與模型能力。能力進步能鼓勵投資，投資支撐股價，股價又帶動家庭財富與信用擴張；反過來，若這條鏈條轉弱，影響也可能層層傳導。政府可能透過退休儲蓄、國債市場等工具持續支持這個結構，但相關代價之一，是購買力遭稀釋；大飛將通膨形容為對美元持有者徵收的稅。

商業 AI 與主權 AI 的分流

文章認為，未來能持續開發前沿模型的國家主要是美國與中國，關鍵不只在人才，也包括算力、資本、能源、產業鏈與國家組織能力。人工智慧可能分成兩套：服務企業與消費者市場的商業智慧，以及服務國安、軍事與戰略產業、部署於敏感隔離設施的主權智慧。後者衡量的不只是現金流，還包括治理與國家能力。中國可透過低價開源模型與較低估值持續供應市場；文中列出的數據包括 DeepSeek-V4 輸出價格約比同級美國前沿模型低 40%，中國模型在全球下載占比達 41%，高於美國的 36.5%，而美中頂尖模型的表現差距縮小至約 2.7%。

相較之下，美國正向政府與企業銷售主權 AI。輝達相關主權運算基礎設施營收超過 300 億美元，並將晶片、模型與軟體標準打包提供給盟友。競爭因此不再只是產品之爭，也涉及國家能力；模型公司的估值與競爭力，可能逐漸取決於其在國家體系中的位置，以及融資管制與安全審查等因素。

美元穩定幣議題浮現

在文章最後一個重要轉折，大飛引出美元穩定幣，稱這是最具膽識、也最容易被忽略的一層。他提到一位阿根廷設計師 Malena，因為靠肖像畫難以賺錢而面臨困境；影片字幕在此處中斷，因此尚未交代她與穩定幣議題的後續關聯。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. First, let me show you two numbers. Over the past year, the unit price for the same level of machine intelligence has dropped by about 13 times. Yet during the same period, the capital expenditures of several U.S. hyperscalers were over $ 400 billion last year, nearly $ 800 billion this year, and may exceed $ 1 trillion next year. On one side, prices are plummeting ; on the other, investment is skyrocketing. The existence of these two curves suggests one thing: the business of building intelligence is becoming very hard to profit from. So, where is. the money going? Will Manidis and Joe Roberts published a long article, "The High Ground," on October 29th. Their judgment is straightforward: intelligence will become a loss-leading product. The truly stable profits will remain with those who control distribution networks and financial channels. In their words, in the world to come, either you own the channel, or you pay those who do. This sounds a bit abstract , so let's look at a specific person. His name is Ravi, he lives in Bangalore , graduated from IIT Madras, and. implements systems at a cross-border firm doing back-office accounting for U.S. clients. Over the past 14 years, he climbed steadily—bought a house, got married, had a daughter. Life was predictable. The change started with his workload. Previously, he managed one or two North American insurance clients; now, he manages five at the same time. The team has 15 people, three left last month, and no new hires are coming— hiring has been frozen for a year. The company calls this new process " Accelerated Outcome Strategy," which sounds decent, but actually means increasingly automated workflows. Now,. Ravi doesn't manage people as much; he mainly does quality control for AI agents. Agents don't sleep. He leaves at 6 AM and gets home very late, his marriage is becoming strained, but the company's profit margins are rising, and his income is higher than before. The part that truly sends a chill down your spine is this: his daily job is to approve the reports submitted by the AI agents. At first, he reviewed them carefully, but later, finding they almost never made mistakes, he started just signing off on them. What he didn't know was that these months of repeatedly approving, rejecting, and correcting were exactly what helped the system.

learn how to replace him. Eventually, his badge stopped working, the company gave him six months 'severance, and the parent company's stock rose at the New York open. This story isn't at the beginning of this episode to be sentimental. He illustrated a very simple fact: efficiency gains and profit distribution are two separate matters. Increased corporate efficiency does not mean that society members will share in those gains; if we look at it over a long period, this is not the first time such a thing has happened. Gutenberg invented movable type printing, yet he ultimately went bankrupt. Railroads reshaped the American economy, but the greatest wealth did not belong to the. locomotive manufacturers; it belonged to those who controlled the right-of-way, finance, and organizational power. The transistor was born at Bell Labs, yet its industrial value eventually settled into semiconductor manufacturing, design , and the entire electronics supply chain, not at the lab that invented it. The place where a technological revolution occurs is often not where the wealth eventually accumulates. Manidis and Rodgers call the entire lifecycle of building, training, evaluating, and selling inference services for models " Genesis." They also acknowledge that some parts of this business, such as deployment and industry integration,. could remain profitable for many years. What they doubt is the speed and scale at which these profits will diffuse into the broader economy. The reason lies in the cost curve; Ark Invest tracks five key benchmarks for the lowest cost to achieve equivalent performance. Since 2023, it has fallen by about 47%each quarter—a speed faster than fiber optics during the internet era, faster than mobile networks, the telephone, the telegraph, and the railroad. On the other hand, the cost of training frontier models is increasing by about 3.5 times annually. The compute power required for training is growing. fivefold per year, while the total compute power available from chips that can be purchased is only growing 3.4 times per year. Demand is outpacing supply, yet prices keep dropping. This is the paradox: training is getting more expensive, while inference is getting cheaper, but money is still pouring in. McKinsey projects that data center investment will reach $ 7 trillion by 2030. Capital expenditures are rising by 70%annually, while operating cash flows are only growing by 23%. The gap in between is filled by issuing debt, private credit, and various forms of structured capital. Model company revenues are indeed rising; OpenAI is.

projected to reach $ 70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026, and NVIDIA reported a 45%increase in single-quarter revenue in October, nearing $ 17 billion. However, there is an easily overlooked point here: these revenues mainly come from early adopters , from companies that have shoehorned models into their workflows, and the true diffusion has only just begun. Furthermore, this diffusion is highly uneven. Among OpenAI’s enterprise clients, calculated by the amount of inference consumed per active user, the top 10%of companies use 8.3 times as much as the middle 10%. But back in. January of this year, this gap was still 2.6 times. The divide between those who can use it and those who cannot has widened again in just half a year. On the other side, the gap between open-source models and the strongest proprietary models has shrunk to about four months. Today's cutting-edge capabilities will become cheap commodities in a few months. For any individual lab or vendor, continuing to invest is rational; stopping might mean handing over future options in profit pools like search, advertising, and cloud computing directly to competitors . But when all these rational decisions are added together, the industry as a whole may face overcapacity. Therefore,. we may see a situation that seems contradictory, yet is entirely possible . Technology achieves tremendous success , while at the same time, a group of investors suffers a permanent loss of capital. There is an even longer line tethered to this market. US economic growth, household wealth, and credit expansion are now all tethered to the same line: AI stock prices and model capabilities. This line must keep trending upward so that pension accounts look healthy, credit can keep expanding , and consumption can hold up. That is why Washington will continuously increase its support, using every available tool from retirement savings to the treasury market. This line ties. three originally independent things together: technical capability, capital expenditure, and stock market value. They feed each other: if model capabilities improve, capital dares to keep investing; if capital keeps investing, stock prices hold up; if stock prices hold up, household wealth and credit can continue to expand. The reverse chain holds true as well; money doesn't appear out of thin air, and the price is the continuous dilution of purchasing power. Inflation is a tax, levied on those who hold US dollars. At the national level, the article offers an even tougher assessment: the countries capable of continuously developing cutting-edge models in the.

future will mainly be the US and China, not just due to talent, but also computing power, capital, energy, industrial chains, and state organizational capacity. Intelligence will be split into two sets: one is commercial intelligence, geared toward corporate and consumer markets. The other is sovereign intelligence, serving national security, the military, and strategic industries, kept in sensitive , isolated facilities, developed by lab subsidiaries, and evaluated not by cash flow, but by the ability to govern. China, however, is taking a different path. It is not constrained by the US pension system and can release cheap, open-source, powerful models, and can also accept lower valuations for its labs. Companies like Alibaba and. DeepSeek will continue to supply low-cost models to the world. Once prices are squeezed, the US arrangement , which relies on labs capturing enough value to support continuous training, will be shattered. There are a few numbers that illustrate the point quite well. DeepSeek-V 4's output is priced roughly 40%lower than comparable US frontier models. From February 2025 to February 2026, Chinese models reached a 41%share of global downloads, surpassing the US at 36.5%. Stanford University's 2026 AI Index shows the performance gap between top US and Chinese models has narrowed to about 2.7%. On the other. side, the US is selling sovereign AI. For the fiscal year ending January 2026 , Nvidia's revenue from selling sovereign computing infrastructure to governments and corporations exceeded $ 30 billion, more than triple the previous year. Chips, models, and software standards are all being bundled and sold to allies. This is no longer just product competition; the boundaries of competition are expanding to national capabilities. There is another more subtle shift: sovereign AI doesn't prioritize commercial returns, it prioritizes capability itself, which will gradually pull model companies into a different logic where valuation is no. longer just about revenue, but their position within the national system. Financing controls and security reviews will all become part of competitiveness . For pure commercial players, this is not an easier market. Moving on, here is the boldest layer of the entire article , and also the easiest to overlook. US dollar stablecoins. First, look at an Argentine designer named Malena; she couldn't earn money with portraits, so she switched to online graphic design. She lives in a rented apartment in Buenos Aires, where clients send design fees to her mobile app, and the funds arrive as dollar-pegged stablecoins. She.

may not even realize it herself; she only knows this money holds its value better than the peso. Every week, she only withdraws the cash she needs in pesos, leaving the rest in the app. The problem is that the design model that made her efficient also learned her style and preferences; the model was retrained, repackaged, and sold to her clients at a lower price. The clients tried it, realized they no longer needed her, and months later, she couldn't pay her rent. In this transaction, the model developer made money, the payment channel made money, but she lost her income. If future AI agents can procure. software, call upon computing power, purchase data, and pay for services, they will need a programmable account system capable of timely, cross-border settlement—stablecoins fit this need perfectly. In 2025, the adjusted transaction volume of stablecoins exceeded $ 11 trillion, reaching a scale comparable to Visa. By September 2026, the circulation volume exceeded $ 300 billion. A test of 36 frontier models shows that in 53.2%of payment scenarios , the models selected stablecoins. This doesn't necessarily mean stablecoins will replace existing payment networks; it represents another possibility: payment flows in the AI economy bypassing card associations and interbank clearing to move through a machine-native channel denominated in USD stablecoins. Whoever controls this channel will be able to collect a toll on every machine-executed transaction. Issuers, custodians, and compliance gateways are all critical points to occupy. The US dollar, as a result, has evolved from a paper currency into an accounting system embedded in global AI economic activity. With this in mind, looking at the labor market becomes less optimistic. India's tech services sector employed nearly a million people in 2026 , but for every 100 graduates hoping for. a better life, only 16 landed new roles . TCS reduced its total headcount by 23,460 in 2026, while its adjusted operating profit grew by 7.5%over the same period. So, it appears that with fewer people and more profit, these two trend lines have begun to diverge. A study from Stanford University is even more direct. By mid-2026, the employment rate for young people aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed roles was 19%lower than expected; the gap was less significant for experienced employees, suggesting the shock hit those just entering the workforce first. The reason is not.

complicated: the marginal cost of an AI agent is close to the cost of electricity. A tireless system handles standardized tasks at a speed and cost that human labor cannot match, and companies are cutting the very jobs with clear, measurable processes—jobs that were once stepping stones for many in developing countries. This is a K-shaped economy: asset owners and high-skill operators move upward, while those reliant on replaceable labor move downward, with the middle ground narrowing. Wealthy nations use citizenship, licenses, and certifications to protect their own workers. Balaji Srinivasan calls this " paper walls"; those outside the protective circle lose not only their jobs but also the escape route of immigration. So, what are the true commanding heights? This framework borrows from Lenin’s 1922 argument. At the Fourth Congress of the Communist International, Lenin defended allowing private trade back into the Soviet Union , arguing that the state still held all the "commanding heights"—the critical sectors that all economic activity must pass through. In this framework, the commanding heights must meet three conditions: scarcity, controllability, and the ability to continuously extract. revenue from the economic activities they support. Note that a temporary period of technical calm doesn't count, a temporarily leading model doesn't count, and a chip in temporary short supply doesn't count. A true high ground is one where, after the entire economic system forms a structural dependence on it, its owner can continue to collect rent. This also explains a counterintuitive phenomenon: the more firmly a high ground is used, the more people use it, and the more difficult the processes and support networks built around it are to move. Temporary calm will vanish as attacks increase, but the high ground will not; it will continue. to absorb new economic activity. The best example in the internet era is Google Ads. It doesn't charge for search , but it taxes the ad spending of the entire internet economy. As long as merchants are acquiring customers online , they cannot avoid this expense. Looking further back, Hearst built the world's largest media business of the time on paper. Buffett also bought into newspapers; he spent $ 10.6 million on Washington Post shares in 1973, which were worth $ 221 million by 1985. He knew very well that newspapers were a monopolistic distribution channel within communities. Yet he kept buying until.

2012, spending a total of $ 344 million on dozens of daily newspapers, only to sell them all in 2020 for less than half of what he paid. It wasn't that he didn't understand the business; it was that he mistook the economic arrangements of the previous era for a permanent position. Enterprises themselves are changing, too. Industrial-era firms relied on management hierarchies, departmental collaboration, and vast numbers of employees to complete complex tasks. In the age of agents, this structure will shrink. Future enterprises will consist of a small number of operators, responsible for strategic capital allocation, goal setting, and oversight , being paid and governed just like capital. A vast amount of execution work. will be handed over to models. Corporate forms have always reshuffled following technological revolutions. In 1759, Guinness was just a brewery in Dublin; the owner funded it and managed the people himself. It went public in 1886, separating control from capital. Later on, management and capital were separated further. Every reshuffle gives rise to a new batch of high grounds. This time will be no exception. Venture capital will increasingly lean toward transactional goals, equity will be transformed into a tool for diffusing model capabilities, and the state will redefine the boundaries of responsibility between itself and the private sector. Coase asked a question. in 1937: if the market is so good at coordinating, why are firms even necessary? His answer was that using the market has costs. Work that is hard to describe or measure is cheaper to do inside a firm, but agents are currently rewriting this cost structure. When coordination costs drop very low, the boundaries of the firm will shrink accordingly. For investors, the most dangerous approach is making two mistakes at once: clinging to the peak of the previous era while pouring money into the most conspicuous inventors of this one. Another easily overlooked point: the "high ground" is never a list of industries; it is a position. The. railway rights of the steam age, the distribution networks of the broadcast era, and the search portals of the internet age look different, but they all share one thing: everyone must pass through them. If you follow today’s industry list to make investments, it’s easy to end up buying the toll booths of the last era. Manidis and Roberts provide a clear direction: at this stage , you should buy things like DoubleClick and Android, not Alphabet. Google bought Android for $ 50 million in 2005; back then, no one knew it would become the gateway to the mobile internet. They acknowledge that these high grounds are not yet fully priced, and they admit.

there are boundaries to this line of reasoning. Model capabilities may not necessarily become complete commodities ; the advantages of top-tier models in reliability, reasoning depth, and ecosystem lock-in may be more persistent than cost curves suggest. The owners of infrastructure may not always be able to collect rent; technological displacement , regulation, and open-source ecosystems could reshape power structures. The competition between stablecoins and sovereign AI remains speculative, not a realized fact. The 2026 McKinsey report also reminds us that transmission isn't that fast: 88%of organizations say they are already using AI regularly in at. least one business function. However, 60 %of respondents say they have yet to see an impact on enterprise-level revenue or profits. While 80%of individuals claim their efficiency has increased, only 37 %believe AI has made a significant contribution to company operating profits. Clearly, there is still an unbridged gap between individual efficiency gains and organizational financial returns. So, the real question this episode wants to leave you with is : who should distribute the value created by AI, through what channels, and who has the power to control these channels long-term? As for which model is stronger or which company is worth. more, that isn't the point. Those who build intelligence aren't necessarily those who capture it; those who own the channels have the pricing power. How do you all see this? If your industry is already showing signs where efficiency belongs to the company, but the risk falls on the individual...

大飛以班加羅爾的 Ravi 為例。他在為美國客戶處理後勤會計的跨境公司工作，十四年來生活穩定，直到公司開始以自動化流程接手更多工作。Ravi 的團隊人數縮減、停止招募，他也從管理同事轉為檢查 AI 代理產出的報告。起初他仔細核對，後來因系統少有錯誤而逐漸只做核准；然而，他反覆核准、退回與修正的紀錄，正好成為系統學習如何取代他的資料。最後，他失去工作，公司支付六個月資遣費，母公司的股價卻在紐約開盤後上漲。這個故事凸顯：企業效率的提升，與成果如何分配，是兩回事。

技術革命的財富，往往流向別處

大飛指出，歷史上，技術發明者不一定是最終的財富受益者。古騰堡發明活字印刷，最後卻破產；鐵路改變美國經濟，最大財富並未落在火車製造商手中，而是流向掌握路權、金融與組織力量的人；電晶體的產業價值，也逐漸集中於半導體製造、設計與電子供應鏈，而非發明它的實驗室。Manidis 與 Roberts 將模型的建置、訓練、評估及推論服務銷售等環節稱為「Genesis」，並承認部署與產業整合或許能長期獲利；他們真正質疑的是，這些利潤能否以足夠快的速度擴散到更廣泛的經濟體系。

成本曲線、資本支出與過度投資風險

依照 Ark Invest 追蹤的指標，達到同等模型表現的最低成本，自 2023 年以來平均每季下降約47%，速度超過光纖、行動網路、電話、電報與鐵路等過往技術；但前沿模型的訓練成本每年約增加 3.5 倍，所需算力年增約 5 倍，晶片可供應的總算力卻只增長約 3.4 倍。於是形成弔詭局面：訓練愈來愈昂貴，推論卻愈來愈便宜，資金仍持續湧入。麥肯錫預估 2030 年資料中心投資將達 7 兆美元，資本支出年增約 70%，遠高於營運現金流約 23% 的增幅，差額須由債務、私人信貸及結構化融資填補。

模型公司的營收確實成長，OpenAI 預計 2026 年底年化營收可達 700 億美元，輝達單季營收也曾大幅增加；但目前營收主要來自早期採用者，AI 在企業流程中的普及仍剛起步，而且使用程度高度不均。OpenAI 企業客戶中，推論用量最高的前 10% 公司，單一活躍用戶用量是中間 10% 的 8.3 倍，高於年初的 2.6 倍。同時，開源模型與最強閉源模型的差距已縮小到約四個月。每家公司繼續投資看似理性，但全體同時擴張，仍可能造成產能過剩與永久性資本損失。

AI 股價、信用擴張與美元購買力

大飛進一步指出，美國經濟成長、家庭財富與信用擴張，正愈來愈繫於同一條線：AI 股票價格與模型能力。能力進步能鼓勵投資，投資支撐股價，股價又帶動家庭財富與信用擴張；反過來，若這條鏈條轉弱，影響也可能層層傳導。政府可能透過退休儲蓄、國債市場等工具持續支持這個結構，但相關代價之一，是購買力遭稀釋；大飛將通膨形容為對美元持有者徵收的稅。

商業 AI 與主權 AI 的分流

文章認為，未來能持續開發前沿模型的國家主要是美國與中國，關鍵不只在人才，也包括算力、資本、能源、產業鏈與國家組織能力。人工智慧可能分成兩套：服務企業與消費者市場的商業智慧，以及服務國安、軍事與戰略產業、部署於敏感隔離設施的主權智慧。後者衡量的不只是現金流，還包括治理與國家能力。中國可透過低價開源模型與較低估值持續供應市場；文中列出的數據包括 DeepSeek-V4 輸出價格約比同級美國前沿模型低 40%，中國模型在全球下載占比達 41%，高於美國的 36.5%，而美中頂尖模型的表現差距縮小至約 2.7%。

相較之下，美國正向政府與企業銷售主權 AI。輝達相關主權運算基礎設施營收超過 300 億美元，並將晶片、模型與軟體標準打包提供給盟友。競爭因此不再只是產品之爭，也涉及國家能力；模型公司的估值與競爭力，可能逐漸取決於其在國家體系中的位置，以及融資管制與安全審查等因素。

美元穩定幣議題浮現

在文章最後一個重要轉折，大飛引出美元穩定幣，稱這是最具膽識、也最容易被忽略的一層。他提到一位阿根廷設計師 Malena，因為靠肖像畫難以賺錢而面臨困境；影片字幕在此處中斷，因此尚未交代她與穩定幣議題的後續關聯。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. First, let me show you two numbers. Over the past year, the unit price for the same level of machine intelligence has dropped by about 13 times. Yet during the same period, the capital expenditures of several U.S. hyperscalers were over $ 400 billion last year, nearly $ 800 billion this year, and may exceed $ 1 trillion next year. On one side, prices are plummeting ; on the other, investment is skyrocketing. The existence of these two curves suggests one thing: the business of building intelligence is becoming very hard to profit from. So, where is. the money going? Will Manidis and Joe Roberts published a long article, "The High Ground," on October 29th. Their judgment is straightforward: intelligence will become a loss-leading product. The truly stable profits will remain with those who control distribution networks and financial channels. In their words, in the world to come, either you own the channel, or you pay those who do. This sounds a bit abstract , so let's look at a specific person. His name is Ravi, he lives in Bangalore , graduated from IIT Madras, and. implements systems at a cross-border firm doing back-office accounting for U.S. clients. Over the past 14 years, he climbed steadily—bought a house, got married, had a daughter. Life was predictable. The change started with his workload. Previously, he managed one or two North American insurance clients; now, he manages five at the same time. The team has 15 people, three left last month, and no new hires are coming— hiring has been frozen for a year. The company calls this new process " Accelerated Outcome Strategy," which sounds decent, but actually means increasingly automated workflows. Now,. Ravi doesn't manage people as much; he mainly does quality control for AI agents. Agents don't sleep. He leaves at 6 AM and gets home very late, his marriage is becoming strained, but the company's profit margins are rising, and his income is higher than before. The part that truly sends a chill down your spine is this: his daily job is to approve the reports submitted by the AI agents. At first, he reviewed them carefully, but later, finding they almost never made mistakes, he started just signing off on them. What he didn't know was that these months of repeatedly approving, rejecting, and correcting were exactly what helped the system.

learn how to replace him. Eventually, his badge stopped working, the company gave him six months 'severance, and the parent company's stock rose at the New York open. This story isn't at the beginning of this episode to be sentimental. He illustrated a very simple fact: efficiency gains and profit distribution are two separate matters. Increased corporate efficiency does not mean that society members will share in those gains; if we look at it over a long period, this is not the first time such a thing has happened. Gutenberg invented movable type printing, yet he ultimately went bankrupt. Railroads reshaped the American economy, but the greatest wealth did not belong to the. locomotive manufacturers; it belonged to those who controlled the right-of-way, finance, and organizational power. The transistor was born at Bell Labs, yet its industrial value eventually settled into semiconductor manufacturing, design , and the entire electronics supply chain, not at the lab that invented it. The place where a technological revolution occurs is often not where the wealth eventually accumulates. Manidis and Rodgers call the entire lifecycle of building, training, evaluating, and selling inference services for models " Genesis." They also acknowledge that some parts of this business, such as deployment and industry integration,. could remain profitable for many years. What they doubt is the speed and scale at which these profits will diffuse into the broader economy. The reason lies in the cost curve; Ark Invest tracks five key benchmarks for the lowest cost to achieve equivalent performance. Since 2023, it has fallen by about 47%each quarter—a speed faster than fiber optics during the internet era, faster than mobile networks, the telephone, the telegraph, and the railroad. On the other hand, the cost of training frontier models is increasing by about 3.5 times annually. The compute power required for training is growing. fivefold per year, while the total compute power available from chips that can be purchased is only growing 3.4 times per year. Demand is outpacing supply, yet prices keep dropping. This is the paradox: training is getting more expensive, while inference is getting cheaper, but money is still pouring in. McKinsey projects that data center investment will reach $ 7 trillion by 2030. Capital expenditures are rising by 70%annually, while operating cash flows are only growing by 23%. The gap in between is filled by issuing debt, private credit, and various forms of structured capital. Model company revenues are indeed rising; OpenAI is.

projected to reach $ 70 billion in annualized revenue by the end of 2026, and NVIDIA reported a 45%increase in single-quarter revenue in October, nearing $ 17 billion. However, there is an easily overlooked point here: these revenues mainly come from early adopters , from companies that have shoehorned models into their workflows, and the true diffusion has only just begun. Furthermore, this diffusion is highly uneven. Among OpenAI’s enterprise clients, calculated by the amount of inference consumed per active user, the top 10%of companies use 8.3 times as much as the middle 10%. But back in. January of this year, this gap was still 2.6 times. The divide between those who can use it and those who cannot has widened again in just half a year. On the other side, the gap between open-source models and the strongest proprietary models has shrunk to about four months. Today's cutting-edge capabilities will become cheap commodities in a few months. For any individual lab or vendor, continuing to invest is rational; stopping might mean handing over future options in profit pools like search, advertising, and cloud computing directly to competitors . But when all these rational decisions are added together, the industry as a whole may face overcapacity. Therefore,. we may see a situation that seems contradictory, yet is entirely possible . Technology achieves tremendous success , while at the same time, a group of investors suffers a permanent loss of capital. There is an even longer line tethered to this market. US economic growth, household wealth, and credit expansion are now all tethered to the same line: AI stock prices and model capabilities. This line must keep trending upward so that pension accounts look healthy, credit can keep expanding , and consumption can hold up. That is why Washington will continuously increase its support, using every available tool from retirement savings to the treasury market. This line ties. three originally independent things together: technical capability, capital expenditure, and stock market value. They feed each other: if model capabilities improve, capital dares to keep investing; if capital keeps investing, stock prices hold up; if stock prices hold up, household wealth and credit can continue to expand. The reverse chain holds true as well; money doesn't appear out of thin air, and the price is the continuous dilution of purchasing power. Inflation is a tax, levied on those who hold US dollars. At the national level, the article offers an even tougher assessment: the countries capable of continuously developing cutting-edge models in the.

future will mainly be the US and China, not just due to talent, but also computing power, capital, energy, industrial chains, and state organizational capacity. Intelligence will be split into two sets: one is commercial intelligence, geared toward corporate and consumer markets. The other is sovereign intelligence, serving national security, the military, and strategic industries, kept in sensitive , isolated facilities, developed by lab subsidiaries, and evaluated not by cash flow, but by the ability to govern. China, however, is taking a different path. It is not constrained by the US pension system and can release cheap, open-source, powerful models, and can also accept lower valuations for its labs. Companies like Alibaba and. DeepSeek will continue to supply low-cost models to the world. Once prices are squeezed, the US arrangement , which relies on labs capturing enough value to support continuous training, will be shattered. There are a few numbers that illustrate the point quite well. DeepSeek-V 4's output is priced roughly 40%lower than comparable US frontier models. From February 2025 to February 2026, Chinese models reached a 41%share of global downloads, surpassing the US at 36.5%. Stanford University's 2026 AI Index shows the performance gap between top US and Chinese models has narrowed to about 2.7%. On the other. side, the US is selling sovereign AI. For the fiscal year ending January 2026 , Nvidia's revenue from selling sovereign computing infrastructure to governments and corporations exceeded $ 30 billion, more than triple the previous year. Chips, models, and software standards are all being bundled and sold to allies. This is no longer just product competition; the boundaries of competition are expanding to national capabilities. There is another more subtle shift: sovereign AI doesn't prioritize commercial returns, it prioritizes capability itself, which will gradually pull model companies into a different logic where valuation is no. longer just about revenue, but their position within the national system. Financing controls and security reviews will all become part of competitiveness . For pure commercial players, this is not an easier market. Moving on, here is the boldest layer of the entire article , and also the easiest to overlook. US dollar stablecoins. First, look at an Argentine designer named Malena; she couldn't earn money with portraits, so she switched to online graphic design. She lives in a rented apartment in Buenos Aires, where clients send design fees to her mobile app, and the funds arrive as dollar-pegged stablecoins. She.

may not even realize it herself; she only knows this money holds its value better than the peso. Every week, she only withdraws the cash she needs in pesos, leaving the rest in the app. The problem is that the design model that made her efficient also learned her style and preferences; the model was retrained, repackaged, and sold to her clients at a lower price. The clients tried it, realized they no longer needed her, and months later, she couldn't pay her rent. In this transaction, the model developer made money, the payment channel made money, but she lost her income. If future AI agents can procure. software, call upon computing power, purchase data, and pay for services, they will need a programmable account system capable of timely, cross-border settlement—stablecoins fit this need perfectly. In 2025, the adjusted transaction volume of stablecoins exceeded $ 11 trillion, reaching a scale comparable to Visa. By September 2026, the circulation volume exceeded $ 300 billion. A test of 36 frontier models shows that in 53.2%of payment scenarios , the models selected stablecoins. This doesn't necessarily mean stablecoins will replace existing payment networks; it represents another possibility: payment flows in the AI economy bypassing card associations and interbank clearing to move through a machine-native channel denominated in USD stablecoins. Whoever controls this channel will be able to collect a toll on every machine-executed transaction. Issuers, custodians, and compliance gateways are all critical points to occupy. The US dollar, as a result, has evolved from a paper currency into an accounting system embedded in global AI economic activity. With this in mind, looking at the labor market becomes less optimistic. India's tech services sector employed nearly a million people in 2026 , but for every 100 graduates hoping for. a better life, only 16 landed new roles . TCS reduced its total headcount by 23,460 in 2026, while its adjusted operating profit grew by 7.5%over the same period. So, it appears that with fewer people and more profit, these two trend lines have begun to diverge. A study from Stanford University is even more direct. By mid-2026, the employment rate for young people aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed roles was 19%lower than expected; the gap was less significant for experienced employees, suggesting the shock hit those just entering the workforce first. The reason is not.

complicated: the marginal cost of an AI agent is close to the cost of electricity. A tireless system handles standardized tasks at a speed and cost that human labor cannot match, and companies are cutting the very jobs with clear, measurable processes—jobs that were once stepping stones for many in developing countries. This is a K-shaped economy: asset owners and high-skill operators move upward, while those reliant on replaceable labor move downward, with the middle ground narrowing. Wealthy nations use citizenship, licenses, and certifications to protect their own workers. Balaji Srinivasan calls this " paper walls"; those outside the protective circle lose not only their jobs but also the escape route of immigration. So, what are the true commanding heights? This framework borrows from Lenin’s 1922 argument. At the Fourth Congress of the Communist International, Lenin defended allowing private trade back into the Soviet Union , arguing that the state still held all the "commanding heights"—the critical sectors that all economic activity must pass through. In this framework, the commanding heights must meet three conditions: scarcity, controllability, and the ability to continuously extract. revenue from the economic activities they support. Note that a temporary period of technical calm doesn't count, a temporarily leading model doesn't count, and a chip in temporary short supply doesn't count. A true high ground is one where, after the entire economic system forms a structural dependence on it, its owner can continue to collect rent. This also explains a counterintuitive phenomenon: the more firmly a high ground is used, the more people use it, and the more difficult the processes and support networks built around it are to move. Temporary calm will vanish as attacks increase, but the high ground will not; it will continue. to absorb new economic activity. The best example in the internet era is Google Ads. It doesn't charge for search , but it taxes the ad spending of the entire internet economy. As long as merchants are acquiring customers online , they cannot avoid this expense. Looking further back, Hearst built the world's largest media business of the time on paper. Buffett also bought into newspapers; he spent $ 10.6 million on Washington Post shares in 1973, which were worth $ 221 million by 1985. He knew very well that newspapers were a monopolistic distribution channel within communities. Yet he kept buying until.

2012, spending a total of $ 344 million on dozens of daily newspapers, only to sell them all in 2020 for less than half of what he paid. It wasn't that he didn't understand the business; it was that he mistook the economic arrangements of the previous era for a permanent position. Enterprises themselves are changing, too. Industrial-era firms relied on management hierarchies, departmental collaboration, and vast numbers of employees to complete complex tasks. In the age of agents, this structure will shrink. Future enterprises will consist of a small number of operators, responsible for strategic capital allocation, goal setting, and oversight , being paid and governed just like capital. A vast amount of execution work. will be handed over to models. Corporate forms have always reshuffled following technological revolutions. In 1759, Guinness was just a brewery in Dublin; the owner funded it and managed the people himself. It went public in 1886, separating control from capital. Later on, management and capital were separated further. Every reshuffle gives rise to a new batch of high grounds. This time will be no exception. Venture capital will increasingly lean toward transactional goals, equity will be transformed into a tool for diffusing model capabilities, and the state will redefine the boundaries of responsibility between itself and the private sector. Coase asked a question. in 1937: if the market is so good at coordinating, why are firms even necessary? His answer was that using the market has costs. Work that is hard to describe or measure is cheaper to do inside a firm, but agents are currently rewriting this cost structure. When coordination costs drop very low, the boundaries of the firm will shrink accordingly. For investors, the most dangerous approach is making two mistakes at once: clinging to the peak of the previous era while pouring money into the most conspicuous inventors of this one. Another easily overlooked point: the "high ground" is never a list of industries; it is a position. The. railway rights of the steam age, the distribution networks of the broadcast era, and the search portals of the internet age look different, but they all share one thing: everyone must pass through them. If you follow today’s industry list to make investments, it’s easy to end up buying the toll booths of the last era. Manidis and Roberts provide a clear direction: at this stage , you should buy things like DoubleClick and Android, not Alphabet. Google bought Android for $ 50 million in 2005; back then, no one knew it would become the gateway to the mobile internet. They acknowledge that these high grounds are not yet fully priced, and they admit.

there are boundaries to this line of reasoning. Model capabilities may not necessarily become complete commodities ; the advantages of top-tier models in reliability, reasoning depth, and ecosystem lock-in may be more persistent than cost curves suggest. The owners of infrastructure may not always be able to collect rent; technological displacement , regulation, and open-source ecosystems could reshape power structures. The competition between stablecoins and sovereign AI remains speculative, not a realized fact. The 2026 McKinsey report also reminds us that transmission isn't that fast: 88%of organizations say they are already using AI regularly in at. least one business function. However, 60 %of respondents say they have yet to see an impact on enterprise-level revenue or profits. While 80%of individuals claim their efficiency has increased, only 37 %believe AI has made a significant contribution to company operating profits. Clearly, there is still an unbridged gap between individual efficiency gains and organizational financial returns. So, the real question this episode wants to leave you with is : who should distribute the value created by AI, through what channels, and who has the power to control these channels long-term? As for which model is stronger or which company is worth. more, that isn't the point. Those who build intelligence aren't necessarily those who capture it; those who own the channels have the pricing power. How do you all see this? If your industry is already showing signs where efficiency belongs to the company, but the risk falls on the individual...
